title: The Morning After Hail in Houston
description: Stay off the roof. Photograph the gutters, screens, and AC fins, then decide whether you need a tarp or an inspection.
html:
The power is back, the kids want to see the dents in the mailbox, and someone has already knocked. The useful work that morning fits in an hour, and none of it requires you on a wet roof.

Walk the ground, not the slope

Wet shingles are slick, and a hail-bruised roof hides soft spots. From the yard, look for missing tabs, a shine where granules used to be, and debris in the valleys. Check window screens for holes, gutters for granule piles, and the outdoor condenser for bent fins. Those metals bruise easier than a shingle. If they are peppered and the roof faces the same direction, you likely have hail even if the ceiling is still dry.

  • Photograph each slope from the ground, plus gutters, downspouts, and screens.
  • Note rooms that had a stain before the storm so you do not blame yesterday for an old leak.
  • Leave the ladder in the garage unless water is actively coming in and you already know how to move on a roof.

When a tarp is the right call

A tarp is for water that is entering the house, not for a roof that merely looks spotted. A sloppy tarp puts dozens of new nail holes in a roof that might have been repairable. If a ceiling is dripping, catch it in a bucket, move what you can, and call for a storm emergency tarp. We fasten so the tarp stays put in the next wind without turning the field of the roof into a pegboard.

If the house is dry, you have time. Storm chasers count on the opposite feeling. Core Four is in Tomball. We will still be here next week.

Who to call, and in what order

Look first. If you see widespread bruising or an active leak, then call your insurer and a roofer who will meet the adjuster. Opening a claim before you know there is damage can still count as a claim on some policies. The Houston homeowner storm checklist walks through the photos worth taking. When you want someone on the roof who is not selling a story, request a free inspection or call (281) 541-0027.
